messages.author: 0ef05797460154a3
messages.subject: calibration
parts:
Hi,

I have a basic question regarding calibration: I tested the same group on different item types and built independent rasch-models for each type. However, the item coefficients, at least for one model, do not have mean zero. How are they calibrated?
I now built a two-factor rasch model, with one factor per item type. Is that preferable to estimating two separate model?
Somewhat differently: Are the item and person parameters estimated at the same time or subsequently?

Thanks a lot in advance!

messages.author: 6a75f6f91a59c568
messages.subject: Re: calibration
parts:
In basic, The Rasch model constrains the slope as 1 to solve item parameter indeterminacy issues. Therefore calibrated person parameter has not mu=0 even the mirt::mirt() uses the MMLE. Moreover, Under the MMLE, if you do not know any item/person parameters, set the prior distribution of the person parameter as \theta~N(0,1); excluding the Rasch model.

Best,
Seongho

Hi,

I have a basic question regarding calibration: I tested the same group on different item types and built independent rasch-models for each type. However, the item coefficients, at least for one model, do not have mean zero. How are they calibrated?
MML, setting the slopes to 1 and estimating the latent variance parameter by default.
I now built a two-factor rasch model, with one factor per item type. Is that preferable to estimating two separate model?
If the factors are correlated, yes. Otherwise, it makes no difference.
Somewhat differently: Are the item and person parameters estimated at the same time or subsequently?

Persons parameters are integrated out via MML estimation. So you'd have to estimate them afterwords with the fscores() function.

Phil

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: calibration
parts:
You need to specify the covariance parameter in the model (mirt assumes the factors are orthogonal by default). There is a COV argument in the mirt.model() syntax which does this. It sounds like for your repeated measures design you just need to fit two separate correlated models: a two-factor model for A-B, and a two-factor model for 1-2. So long as there are no cross-loadings then you'll obtain the same results, however you'll avoid having to evaluate 4-dimensional integrals (which starts to get inaccurate and slow). 

Phil

I'd probably go with the 'nlminb' optimizer. It's noticeably slower, but tends to be more stable. That particular error message is quite common, and something I've had to hack at in the past to get around. If you still are having issues feel free to send me a reproducible example and I'll try and make a patch. 

Phil
